questions.text: Explain how you would optimise rendering of a large list (10,000+ rows) in a React application.
questions.reference_answer: Use windowing / virtualization (react-window or react-virtualized) so only visible rows are mounted. Provide stable, unique key props. Memoize row components with React.memo. Avoid inline objects / functions in props to prevent re-renders. Debounce scroll handlers. If data comes from an API, paginate or use infinite scroll.

questions.text: What is the Virtual DOM and how does React use it to update the UI efficiently?
questions.reference_answer: The Virtual DOM is an in-memory representation of the real DOM. On state/props change, React builds a new VDOM tree, diffs it against the previous one (reconciliation), and computes a minimal set of real-DOM mutations to apply. This batching + diffing is faster than direct DOM manipulation for most UI updates.

score_3: defines Virtual DOM but no diffing detail

questions.text: Compare useState, useReducer, and Redux. When would you choose each?
questions.reference_answer: useState: simple local component state. useReducer: complex local state with multiple sub-values or transitions best expressed as actions. Redux (or Redux Toolkit): app-wide shared state across many components, with middleware, devtools, and predictable global state. Prefer Context + useReducer for medium apps; Redux for large apps with cross-cutting state.

score_5: clearly separates local vs global state

questions.text: How do you handle authentication tokens (JWT) securely on the frontend?
questions.reference_answer: Prefer HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies so JS cannot read the token (mitigates XSS). If storing in memory, keep tokens out of localStorage (XSS-exposed). Attach tokens via Authorization header on each API call using an interceptor. Refresh tokens via a short-lived access token + refresh token flow. Always use HTTPS.

score_5: warns against localStorage due to XSS
recommends HttpOnly + Secure cookies OR in-memory storage
mentions axios/fetch interceptor or Authorization header
score_0: recommends storing tokens in localStorage without caveat

questions.text: Explain the CSS Box Model and the difference between content-box and border-box.
questions.reference_answer: The box model is content + padding + border + margin. With content-box (default), width/height apply only to content and padding/border add to total size. With border-box, width/height include padding and border, so total size stays predictable. Most modern resets set box-sizing: border-box globally.

explains content-box vs border-box width calculation
score_3: explains box model but not the two sizing modes

questions.text: What are React hooks rules, and what happens if you call a hook conditionally?
questions.reference_answer: Rules: (1) only call hooks at the top level, never inside loops/conditions/nested functions, and (2) only call from React function components or custom hooks. React relies on the call order to associate state with the correct hook slot. Calling conditionally shifts the order, corrupts state mapping, and typically triggers a lint / runtime error.

score_3: states rules but not the reason
score_0: claims hooks can be called anywhere

questions.text: Explain Dependency Injection in Spring. What is the difference between constructor, setter, and field injection, and which is preferred?
questions.reference_answer: DI lets Spring supply collaborators to a bean rather than the bean creating them. Constructor injection: dependencies passed via constructor; enables final fields, easy unit testing, and fails fast if a bean is missing. Setter injection: via setters, useful for optional dependencies. Field injection (@Autowired on a field): concise but hides dependencies, complicates testing, and is discouraged. Constructor injection is preferred.

score_3: names the three types but no reasoning

questions.text: What is the difference between @Controller and @RestController in Spring, and how does @RequestMapping / @GetMapping work?
questions.reference_answer: @Controller returns view names resolved by a ViewResolver (e.g., Thymeleaf). @RestController is @Controller + @ResponseBody, so return values are serialized directly (JSON) into the HTTP body. @RequestMapping maps URLs to handler methods; @GetMapping, @PostMapping etc. are shortcuts for specific HTTP verbs.

score_3: identifies REST vs MVC but no mention of @ResponseBody

questions.text: Explain JPA / Hibernate entity lifecycle states (Transient, Persistent, Detached, Removed) and the role of the EntityManager / Session.
questions.reference_answer: Transient: new object, not associated with a persistence context. Persistent: managed by the current EntityManager/Session; changes are auto-synced on flush. Detached: was persistent but the context closed; changes are not tracked until re-attached via merge(). Removed: scheduled for deletion on flush. EntityManager (JPA) / Session (Hibernate) is the persistence context that tracks entities and coordinates flush/commit.

score_5: explains what triggers transitions (persist, merge, remove, close)
defines role of EntityManager / persistence context

questions.text: How would you design a REST API endpoint that handles concurrent updates to the same resource without lost updates?
questions.reference_answer: Use optimistic locking with a @Version column: each update compares the version; a mismatch throws OptimisticLockException and the client retries. Alternatively use pessimistic locking (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) for high-contention rows. Return HTTP 409 Conflict on version mismatch. Use idempotency keys for POST/PUT retries. ETags + If-Match headers are the HTTP-native way to do the same.

score_5: returns 409 Conflict or uses ETag / If-Match

questions.text: What is the difference between checked and unchecked exceptions in Java, and how would you handle exceptions in a Spring Boot REST controller?
questions.reference_answer: Checked exceptions (extend Exception, not RuntimeException) must be declared or caught; used for recoverable conditions. Unchecked (RuntimeException) are for programming errors. In Spring Boot, centralize handling with @RestControllerAdvice + @ExceptionHandler methods that map exceptions to a consistent JSON error body and appropriate HTTP status. Avoid catching and swallowing; log with correlation IDs.

score_5: maps exceptions to HTTP status codes
score_3: mentions try/catch but no global handler

questions.text: Explain how you would secure a Spring Boot REST API with JWT-based authentication.
questions.reference_answer: Add Spring Security. Configure a stateless SecurityFilterChain (session policy STATELESS). On /login, validate credentials and issue a signed JWT (HS256/RS256) with claims (sub, roles, exp). Add a JwtAuthenticationFilter before UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter that extracts the Bearer token, verifies signature and expiry, and sets Authentication in SecurityContext. Use @PreAuthorize for method-level authorization. Keep secrets in env vars; use short-lived access + refresh tokens.

score_5: describes a custom JWT filter and SecurityContext
mentions refresh token flow or method-level security
score_3: mentions JWT and Spring Security but no filter chain detail

questions.text: Explain the difference between a list, tuple, set, and dict in Python. When would you use each?
questions.reference_answer: list: ordered, mutable, allows duplicates — for sequences that change. tuple: ordered, immutable — for fixed records or dict keys. set: unordered, unique elements — for membership tests and dedup. dict: key-value map, keys hashable and unique — for lookups by key. Choose by mutability, order, and lookup pattern.

questions.text: What is the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) in CPython? How does it affect multithreading and multiprocessing?
questions.reference_answer: The GIL is a mutex in CPython that allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time. CPU-bound multithreading gets no true parallelism — use multiprocessing (separate interpreters/processes) or C-extensions that release the GIL. I/O-bound work still benefits from threads because the GIL is released during blocking I/O. asyncio is a single-thread cooperative alternative for I/O-bound concurrency.

score_5: correctly defines the GIL and CPython-specific nature
explains impact on CPU-bound vs I/O-bound work
score_3: defines GIL but not CPU vs I/O impact

questions.text: How do decorators work in Python? Write a decorator that logs the execution time of a function.
questions.reference_answer:
A decorator is a callable that takes a function and returns a new function, usually wrapping the original to add behavior. Use functools.wraps to preserve metadata. Example: def timer(fn):
  @wraps(fn)
  def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    result = fn(*args, **kwargs)
    print(f'{fn.__name__} took {time.perf_counter()-start:.3f}s')
    return result
  return wrapper

score_3: explains concept but code has minor bugs
score_0: code does not call the wrapped function

questions.text: Compare FastAPI, Flask, and Django. Which would you choose for a modern async REST API and why?
questions.reference_answer: Flask: minimal WSGI microframework; flexible but you assemble everything. Django: batteries-included (ORM, admin, auth) — great for CRUD-heavy apps but heavier. FastAPI: modern ASGI, native async/await, Pydantic-based validation, auto OpenAPI docs, type-hint driven. For a modern async REST API, FastAPI is the best fit due to performance, async support, and automatic docs.

questions.text: Explain generators and the difference between yield and return. When are generators preferable to lists?
questions.reference_answer: A generator function uses yield; calling it returns a generator object that produces values lazily on each next() call, retaining local state between yields. return in a normal function returns a single value and ends execution. Generators are preferable when the data is large or infinite, streamed, or produced on demand — memory usage stays O(1) instead of O(n).

score_5: explains lazy evaluation and state retention
score_3: defines yield but not the lazy/state aspect
score_0: claims yield is the same as return

questions.text: How would you handle database transactions and connection pooling in a FastAPI + SQLAlchemy application?
questions.reference_answer: Configure a SQLAlchemy Engine with a connection pool (pool_size, max_overflow, pool_pre_ping). Use a scoped SessionLocal factory. Provide a FastAPI dependency that yields a session and closes it in a finally block (or uses async context). Wrap unit-of-work operations in session.begin() so commit/rollback are automatic on exception. For async, use AsyncEngine + AsyncSession. Never share a session across requests.

score_5: uses FastAPI dependency to scope session per request
score_3: creates session per request but no pool config
manual commit only, no rollback path
score_0: creates a global session shared across requests
